title: Matsushita's Unsold Socket and the Order for Fan Insulator Plates
dek: In 1917 a young inspector quit his job to make a socket nobody bought, and a modest order for another firm's fan parts kept him going.

story.company: Matsushita Electric Housewares Manufacturing Works (later Panasonic)
story.event: Surviving an unsold light socket by making fan insulator plates, then launching an attachment plug and two-way socket
story.summary: In 1917 Konosuke Matsushita left the Osaka Electric Light Company to make an improved light socket his supervisor had dismissed; working from a two-room tenement with his wife Mumeno and her brother Toshio Iue, he sold almost none. An order for insulator plates for electric fans kept the venture alive, and on 7 March 1918 he founded Matsushita Electric Housewares Manufacturing Works, whose attachment plug and two-way socket sold well enough that it employed 20 people by the end of the year.
paragraphs: In 1917 Konosuke Matsushita was 22 and an inspector at the Osaka Electric Light Company, which he had joined at 15 as a wiring assistant. He had designed an improved light socket and, the year before, applied to register the design. When he showed his supervisor a sample, Panasonic's history records, he was told it was useless and that nothing would come of it. His health was poor, and he decided to leave and make the socket himself.

In June 1917 he set up in a two-room tenement in Ikaino, in eastern Osaka, with his wife, Mumeno, and her younger brother, Toshio Iue, who would later found Sanyo. They managed to produce the socket, but almost nobody bought it. One reference account says wholesalers told him a single product was not enough to interest them. Money ran so short that Mumeno made repeated trips to the pawnshop to pay for necessities.

Towards the end of the year a large manufacturer asked him to make insulator plates for electric fans: a part for someone else's product, not his own idea. He took the work, and the company history says he filled the order quickly and carefully. Repeat orders followed. On 7 March 1918 the three of them moved into a rented two-storey house in Ohiraki-cho, turned the ground floor into a workshop with two hand-operated presses, and founded Matsushita Electric Housewares Manufacturing Works. Production began with fan plates, while Matsushita worked late at night on fixtures of his own.

He chose two: an attachment plug, which let an appliance draw power from a ceiling light socket, and a two-way socket. For the plug's screw-in metal part he reused the bases of spent light bulbs, which already fitted the sockets and, as waste, were cheap. Panasonic's accounts put the products at 30 per cent, or 30 to 50 per cent, cheaper than others on the market. They sold, and by the end of 1918 the workshop employed 20 people. When rivals' price cutting broke his arrangement with a single wholesaler, he began selling to other wholesalers directly, and the business steadied.

quote.text: in all your affairs accept with a good grace what you can and decline what you feel you cannot do. Whatever it be, do it heart and soul, and make it your finest work.
quote.locator: Book II, Chapter VIII (Socrates to Eutherus)
quote.source_title: The Memorabilia, tr. Henry Graham Dakyns, Project Gutenberg eBook #1177
quote.connection: Socrates said this to Eutherus, a friend left poor by war who refused work that would make him answerable to another man. The advice treats a job taken out of need, on someone else's terms, as a place for one's best work rather than a humiliation to be endured.

reflection: There is a quiet kind of pride that treats paid work for someone else as a detour from the real thing. Matsushita's real thing, the socket, had not sold. What carried him to the plug and the two-way socket was a modest part for another firm's fans, made properly, and the presses and practice it paid for.

You may have work like that: a shift, a contract, a favour for another department that keeps the household running while your own idea waits. It does not have to be resented to be temporary. Doing it well is part of how the other thing gets built, and on some days it is enough.
invitation: Pick one task today that you are doing for someone else only because you must. Do it carefully and finish it, then note one thing it taught you that you could use in your own work.

research_notes: Price advantage: Panasonic's 1918 chronicle and ITmedia's museum report say the plug and socket were 30 to 50 per cent cheaper; Panasonic's 2026 Episode 07 says the plug was 30 per cent cheaper; the Gale entry says almost 50 per cent. The story gives Panasonic's two figures side by side. Founding team: Panasonic, PHP and Entrepreneur name three people (Matsushita, Mumeno, Toshio Iue); Gale says his wife and three assistants; widely repeated secondary accounts mention two former colleagues who left by the end of 1917, but no loaded source confirms that, so the story names only the three and does not say they were the only ones. The rescuing customer is unnamed in Panasonic's English chronicle (the name is missing from the sentence); Japanese secondary accounts name the fan maker Kawakita Denki and give an order of 1,000 plates, an 80-yen profit and a second order for 2,000, but none of those figures appears in a source cited here, so the story says only 'a large manufacturer' and 'repeat orders'. EBSCO's account instead credits an early attachment plug with a profit of about forty dollars before the founding; the story follows Panasonic's own sequence (fan plates first, plug after March 1918). Capital: accounts give 'less than 100 yen', 'about one hundred dollars' and other figures; the story avoids a number. Dates: the PHP timeline puts the socket design application in 1916 and the inspector promotion and resignation in 1917; the National Diet Library portrait says he devised the improved socket in 1917; the story says he had designed it and applied to register it the year before he left. Gale's entry calls the first product an 'electric plug' where Panasonic says socket; the story follows Panasonic. ITmedia is in Japanese, so the verifier sees it as live but not naming the founder in Latin script. The quote is Socrates' advice, reported by Xenophon, to Eutherus, who had lost his property abroad after the Peloponnesian War; it ends before the translator's footnote marker '(4)'.
